opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I like to think about it is in terms of two numbers: the branching factor and the depth. In Go you've got a 19-by-19 board, so 361 intersections. On any given move early in the game you have something like two to three hundred legal moves, and a typical game runs maybe 150 to 250 moves. So if you naively expand that tree, you're looking at something like 250 to the power of 150. That's roughly 10 to the 360. People like to say it's more than the number of atoms in the universe, which is around 10 to the 80, but honestly that comparison undersells it. It's not just bigger, it's absurdly, incomprehensibly bigger. Even the number of legal board positions alone is around 10 to the 170.

Compare that to chess, where the branching factor is about 35 and games are maybe 80 plies. That's still enormous, but chess engines could get pretty far with alpha-beta pruning and handcrafted evaluation functions, because you could search deep enough and the position features were legible enough for humans to write down.

Go breaks both of those crutches. The breadth is too wide to search exhaustively, and the depth is too long to just roll out to the end and see who won. Writing a good evaluation function by hand is notoriously hard, because whether a group is alive or dead, or whether some influence in the center will pay off fifty moves later, is very subtle.

So the real insight behind AlphaGo, and especially AlphaZero, is that you attack each dimension with a neural network. The policy network cuts the breadth. Instead of considering 250 moves, you focus on the handful a strong player would plausibly consider, so the effective branching factor collapses. The value network cuts the depth. Instead of simulating to the end of the game, you stop at some point and ask the network, "From here, who's likely to win?" Monte Carlo tree search glues the two together, spending its compute on the promising lines.

What I find beautiful is that the tree doesn't actually get smaller. It's still 10 to the 360. You've just learned an intuition for which tiny sliver of it is worth looking at. I think that's a pretty general lesson for AI: you rarely beat a combinatorial explosion by brute force. You beat it by learning priors that make most of the space irrelevant.

r001.rationale: The candidate estimates about 250^150 (roughly 10^360) sequences, not an estimate on the order of 361^300.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the number everyone quotes is that the game tree for Go has something like 10 to the 170 possible positions, which is more than the number of atoms in the observable universe by a huge margin. And that number is true, but I think it's a little bit of a red herring for how to actually think about the problem.

The naive way to think about it is: there are about 250 legal moves at each turn, games go on for maybe 150 moves, so you get 250 to the 150. And if you imagine trying to brute-force that with minimax, you're obviously never going to get anywhere. That's why for a long time people said Go was the Everest of board games, that it wouldn't fall to computers for decades.

But the thing that AlphaGo really showed is that the size of the raw tree doesn't matter nearly as much as how well you can prune it. The tree is enormous, but the vast majority of it is garbage. Almost all of those positions are ones that no competent player would ever reach, because you'd have to play a bunch of terrible moves to get there. So the effective branching factor, once you have a good policy network telling you "these are the three or four moves that actually make sense here," collapses dramatically. You're no longer searching 250 moves deep, you're searching a handful, and Monte Carlo tree search lets you allocate your compute to the branches that matter.

The other thing is the value function. If you can look at a board and get a decent estimate of who's winning without playing it out, you don't need to search to the end of the game at all. You can truncate the search at a reasonable depth and trust your evaluation. So the depth collapses too.

So the way I'd frame it is: the tree is astronomically large, but intelligence is essentially the ability to not look at most of it. Humans do this too. A professional player isn't searching the tree, they're using pattern recognition, intuition, to narrow it to a few candidate moves and then reading out those lines fairly deeply. AlphaGo basically learned to do the same thing, just with a lot more compute behind the reading.

And honestly I think that's the more general lesson for AI, not just Go. The world is combinatorially huge in the same way. Robotics, for example, the space of possible action sequences is way bigger than Go. But you don't solve that by searching. You solve it by learning good priors that make the search tractable, or make search unnecessary altogether. The scale of the tree tells you the problem is hard in principle. The quality of your learned heuristics tells you whether it's hard in practice.

r001.rationale: The response estimates the naive tree as roughly 250^150 and mentions 10^170 possible positions; it does not estimate 361^300 move sequences.

astra-6.text:
The striking thing about Go is that the search tree is so large that brute force is hopeless. You have hundreds of possible moves at each step, and a game can last hundreds of moves. So even if you had vastly more compute, you couldn’t enumerate all the possible games.

What makes it tractable is learning which branches deserve attention. A policy network says, “These moves look promising,” and a value network says, “This position looks good,” without having to play every continuation to the end. Then search spends its budget exploring the possibilities that matter. You’re using learned intuition to make an otherwise impossible search manageable.

r001.rationale: The response says Go has hundreds of possible moves over hundreds of moves, making exhaustive search impractical, but it does not estimate the tree as on the order of 361³⁰⁰ move sequences.

sol-6.1.text:
The game tree for Go is unimaginably large. You have a 19-by-19 board, so there are 361 possible opening moves, then roughly 360 responses, and so on. Not every sequence is legal, and games don’t necessarily fill the board, but you’re still talking about something like 10 to the 360 possible games. There’s no hope of exhaustively searching that.

But the interesting thing is that you don’t need to. A strong player looks at a position and immediately rules out almost every move. AlphaGo does something similar: its policy network suggests promising moves, and its value network estimates how good a position is without having to play out every continuation. Search then concentrates computation on a tiny fraction of the tree. So the raw size is enormous, but what matters is how much structure you can learn that lets you avoid searching most of it.

r001.rationale: The response estimates about 10^360 possible games, not on the order of 361^300 move sequences (about 10^767).
